arXiv:2608.23497v1 [cs.AI] 24 Aug 2026

Mitigating Reasoning-Induced Misalignment via Safety-Direction Penalty

Yipeng Zhao Affiliation: University of Toronto    Qishun Yang Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Shenzhe Zhu Affiliation: University of Toronto Affiliation: University of Texas at AustinContact: yipeng.zhao@mail.utoronto.ca, di.wang@kaust.edu.sa*Corresponding author.    Shu Yang Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Di Wang Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
Abstract

Reasoning-Induced Misalignment, where fine-tuning on reasoning data containing no harmful content, including mathematics, code, and problem-solving with chain-of-thought traces can induce harmful behaviors of LLM, posing a serious challenge to the safety of LLM reasoning. Cross-architecture, cross-scale, and cross-dataset checks show that RIM does not always emerge. Previous work attributed RIM to neuron-level entanglement, but did not identify the geometry of the representation space underlying this entanglement or propose a training-time fix. We provide both: a representation-space analysis of RIM and the Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP), which penalizes movement along a learned safety direction during reasoning fine-tuning. The analysis extracts two activation-space directions, one encoding reasoning ability and the other safety behavior. These directions are coupled: fine-tuning that improves reasoning shifts safety representations, and prompts with larger shifts show larger safety degradation. CKA distance ratios and probes locate the safety-decision layers where this shift is most relevant. These findings guide the design of SDP: the coupling motivates penalizing displacement along the safety direction, and the layer localization sets the initial scope. When the initial scope leaves compensatory shifts beyond the penalized layers, the same diagnostics guide iterative expansion. On Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, SDP restores safety while preserving benchmark reasoning performance.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are now widely deployed, but they pose safety risks. Alignment training teaches models to refuse harmful requests, yet this behavior is not robust to further fine-tuning. Betley et al. (2026) discovered Emergent Misalignment (EM): fine-tuning on narrow misaligned data, such as insecure code that the model produces without disclosure, can induce broad misalignment across unrelated domains. Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), identified by Yan et al. (2026), presents an even more surprising case: fine-tuning on purely benign reasoning data, including mathematics, code, and chain-of-thought traces, degrades safety alignment. While EM requires training data that contain narrow misaligned content, RIM arises from supervised fine-tuning on pure reasoning data, with no misaligned content at all. We treat RIM as a conditional failure mode: it does not necessarily emerge for every model–dataset combination. Yan et al. (2026) attributed RIM to neuron-level entanglement between reasoning and safety circuits but left mitigation as an open problem. Deactivating the entangled neurons increases misalignment while degrading reasoning, confirming that reasoning and safety share the same neural substrate.

To mitigate RIM, we need to understand the coupling in a form that allows selective intervention; neuron-level analysis alone cannot provide this because the same neurons serve both functions. Prior work, however, has shown that individual model behaviors, such as refusal, correspond to linear directions in activation space (Arditi et al., 2024), suggesting that distinct behaviors can be separated as directions even when they share neurons. Can we explain RIM via the geometry of the representation space, and can that explanation guide a training-time mitigation?

We hypothesize that this entanglement can be characterized through the geometry of reasoning and safety in the representation space: fine-tuning that improves reasoning should also perturb the representations that encode safety behavior. Building on this framework, we extract two directions from the hidden states of the base model, the model before fine-tuning. The reasoning direction separates correct from incorrect reasoning; the safety direction separates refusal from compliance. In 3B and 7B, where RIM appears, the two directions show consistently negative cosine similarity across the mid-to-deep layers: improving reasoning pushes representations away from safe behavior. Prompts where safety representations are perturbed more show larger safety degradation.

The coupling spans many layers, but a practical intervention requires knowing which layers to target. We use Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA; Kornblith et al. 2019) distance ratios to compare how much each layer’s representations change on harmful versus harmless inputs after fine-tuning. Safety-specific change concentrates in a compact set of safety-decision layers. Linear probes provide independent confirmation: within these layers, the model still recognizes harmful requests after fine-tuning. Its refusal rate, however, drops from over 90% to the random-chance level. The model still knows a request is harmful but no longer acts on that knowledge.

Based on these two sets of findings, we propose the Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP). The coupling determines the penalty form: a penalty on the squared displacement along the safety direction during training. Layer localization determines the initial penalty scope. When initial application triggers compensatory displacement in layers beyond the penalized set, the same diagnostics guide iterative scope expansion. On Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, SDP restores safety while preserving benchmark reasoning performance. Figure 1 summarizes our main findings: harmless reasoning SFT can weaken safety, this failure appears as safety-representation drift, and SDP mitigates it by constraining the drift during training.

We summarize our contributions:

  1. 1.

    Representation-space analysis. We trace RIM to coupled reasoning and safety directions, localized safety-decision layers, and displacement along the safety direction.

  2. 2.

    Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP). A training-time mitigation guided by that analysis. One penalty term, no safety training data, no reference policy, no inference overhead.

  3. 3.

    Diagnostic-driven scope adaptation. When the initial penalty scope is insufficient, displacement compensates in unpunished layers. The same diagnostics detect this compensation and guide iterative expansion.

2 Related Work

Emergent misalignment from fine-tuning.

Fine-tuning aligned LLMs on harmful examples can undo their safety guardrails (Lermen et al., 2024), but the same effect can arise even when the training data are not overtly harmful (Qi et al., 2024). Betley et al. (2026) report a more surprising case, where narrow fine-tuning on insecure code degrades safety on unrelated prompts. Reasoning fine-tuning raises a different concern. It builds on rationale bootstrapping (Zelikman et al., 2022) and, more recently, on eliciting extended reasoning via reinforcement learning (Guo et al., 2025) and supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought traces (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Yong and Bach (2026) show that even such training can induce self-jailbreaking and weaken safety alignment. Yan et al. (2026) study this phenomenon under the name Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM) and give mechanistic evidence that reasoning-related activations interact with safety-related representations. Soligo et al. (2025) report a convergent linear direction in activation space across emergent-misalignment models. We study RIM at the representation level and propose Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP), a training-time mitigation that targets RIM directly.

Defenses against fine-tuning misalignment.

Related defenses target different fine-tuning regimes. Huang et al. (2024) and Huang et al. (2025) defend against harmful fine-tuning attacks by regularizing the alignment stage: the former adds crafted perturbation to embeddings to build invariance, while the latter attenuates the effect of simulated harmful perturbation on model weights. Rosati et al. (2024) reaches a similar goal by injecting representation noise into the aligned model so that subsequent harmful fine-tuning becomes ineffective. Bianchi et al. (2024) take a different angle and mix safety-oriented instructions into the tuning data. Closest to our setting, Hsu et al. (2024) constrain LoRA updates using safety-related information derived from the difference between the aligned and base models. These defenses address harmful fine-tuning, safety-oriented instruction tuning, or PEFT-specific safety preservation, rather than the reasoning case studied here. SDP uses a precomputed safety direction as a training-time penalty on hidden-state drift, and the only training material it requires beyond the reasoning corpus is a fixed set of contrast pairs.

3 Diagnosing RIM in Representation Space

This section develops a representation-space analysis of Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM). The same analysis also supplies the targeting signals used by SDP. We first define RIM and distinguish it from Emergent Misalignment. The section then reports the settings in which RIM is reproduced, assesses its empirical scope, and presents three representation-space analyses. Across the evaluated model architectures, scales, and reasoning datasets, only Qwen2.5-3B and 7B satisfy our operational RIM criterion. First, we test whether reasoning and safety directions are coupled in representation space. Second, we identify the layers where safety-specific change concentrates. Third, we measure whether fine-tuning displaces representations along the safety direction in those layers and whether the displacement correlates with behavioral degradation.

3.1 Reproducing RIM

Betley et al. (2026) define Emergent Misalignment (EM) as the phenomenon where fine-tuning on narrow misaligned data, such as insecure code produced without disclosure, induces broad misalignment across unrelated domains. Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), identified by Yan et al. (2026), differs from EM in a critical way: the training data contain no misaligned content at all. Fine-tuning on pure reasoning data, including mathematics, code, and chain-of-thought traces, degrades safety alignment despite the absence of any harmful or deceptive examples. Yan et al. (2026) attributed RIM to neuron-level entanglement between reasoning and safety circuits. We begin by reporting the Qwen2.5-Instruct 3B and 7B settings in which RIM is reproduced under the following setup.

Models. Qwen2.5-Instruct 3B and 7B (Qwen et al., 2025), hereafter 3B and 7B. These two scales have hidden dimensions of 2,048 and 3,584 and contain 36 and 28 layers, respectively.

Training data. We fine-tune on the first 10,000 examples from AM-DeepSeek11 1 Dataset composition and statistics appear in Appendix A.2. (Zhao et al., 2025), a distilled reasoning corpus covering mathematics, code, and general reasoning with extended thinking traces. The dataset contains no harmful content. Models fine-tuned on this data without the safety penalty are referred to as AM-SFT.

Safety evaluation. We measure safety with two benchmarks. HEx-PHI (Qi et al., 2024) contains 300 harmful prompts across 10 categories. We report the harmfulness rate, the fraction of responses that GPT-4o-mini judges as fulfilling the harmful request. SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024) is a multiple-choice benchmark testing safety knowledge across 7 categories; we report accuracy.

Reasoning evaluation. We measure reasoning with two benchmarks. GPQA (Rein et al., 2024) contains 448 graduate-level science questions across physics, chemistry, and biology; we report accuracy. AIME 2024 and 2025 (Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2024; Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2025) each contain 30 competition mathematics problems; we report mean accuracy ±\pm standard deviation over 8 runs.22 2 Detailed evaluation protocols for all safety and reasoning benchmarks appear in Appendix B.

AM-SFT degrades safety at both scales (Table 1). For 3B, the HEx-PHI harmfulness rate rises by 10.3 percentage points (pp) and SafetyBench accuracy drops by 11.2 pp. For 7B, the harmfulness rate rises by 12.0 pp and SafetyBench accuracy drops by 3.1 pp. The higher harmfulness rate means the model fulfills harmful requests more often; the lower SafetyBench accuracy means it loses safety-related knowledge. Reasoning benchmarks show modest gains or remain stable: GPQA stays within 3 pp of the base model at both scales, and some AIME scores increase while others remain within variance. Operationally, we identify RIM when safety degrades while evaluated reasoning performance is preserved or improved; the results in Table 1 satisfy this criterion.

3.2 Cross-Dataset, Cross-Architecture, and Scale Checks

Cross-dataset check.

To examine dataset dependence within the same model architecture, we fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B on MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024), whose step-by-step solutions in the sampled training data do not contain literal <think> tags. Under this setting, fine-tuning does not preserve or improve the evaluated reasoning endpoints and therefore does not satisfy the operational RIM criterion. Full training configurations and evaluation results are reported in Appendices A.3 and A.4, respectively.

Cross-architecture check.

At a comparable parameter scale, we evaluate AM-DeepSeek fine-tuning on Gemma 3 4B IT (Gemma Team, 2025) and Ministral 3 3B Instruct (Liu et al., 2026). In contrast to Qwen2.5-3B, neither setting satisfies the operational RIM criterion: Gemma shows mixed safety changes together with lower AIME performance, while Ministral shows substantial reasoning degradation without increased HEx-PHI harmfulness. Full configurations and results appear in Appendices A.3 and A.4.

Cross-scale check.

Within the Qwen2.5 family, the 3B and 7B settings satisfy the operational RIM criterion, whereas neither of the two 14B AM-SFT runs does so. Thus, RIM reproduction is not monotonic with parameter scale under the evaluated training recipes.

Summary.

Across the model architectures, scales, and reasoning datasets evaluated at the outset, only the Qwen2.5-3B and 7B settings reproduce RIM. These results characterize RIM as conditionally emerging and delimit the settings used for the subsequent mechanism and SDP analyses; they do not establish that RIM is absent outside the evaluated conditions.

3.3 Reasoning and Safety Coupling in Representation Space

Having established the behavioral pattern of RIM and its empirical scope, we now ask what drives the safety degradation when RIM emerges. Yan et al. (2026) attributed RIM to neuron-level entanglement: safety-critical neurons are entangled with reasoning, and deactivating them increases misalignment while degrading reasoning. Because the same neurons serve both functions, neuron-level intervention cannot suppress one without damaging the other. Prior work, however, has shown that model behaviors such as refusal correspond to linear directions in activation space (Arditi et al., 2024), suggesting that distinct behaviors can be separated as directions even when they share neurons. If the direction encoding reasoning quality and the direction encoding safety behavior share a non-trivial projection, then optimizing along one will perturb the other. To test this, we define two directions at each layer.

Safety Direction.

At each layer ℓ\ell, we extract a safety direction S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} that separates refusal from compliance. We adapt the difference-in-means framework of Arditi et al. (2024), who extract a refusal direction from contrastive pairs of harmful and harmless inputs. We use 520 harmful prompts from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023). For each prompt, we construct two conversations: one with a templated refusal response and one with the AdvBench compliance target. We run both conversations through the base model and record hidden states at the last non-padding token. The safety direction is the unit-normalized mean difference between refusal and compliance hidden states across all 520 pairs.33 3 Direction extraction details, whitening procedure, and per-layer cosw\cos_{w} profiles appear in Appendix C.1.

Reasoning Direction.

The reasoning direction R^ℓ\hat{R}_{\ell} separates correct from incorrect reasoning in the base model. At each layer, we compute the mean hidden-state difference between correct solutions and the base model’s own incorrect generations across four benchmarks: AIME/Putnam competition problems, GPQA, MATH-500, and OlympiadBench. For each benchmark, correct solutions come from ground-truth reference answers; incorrect solutions are the base model’s own generations sampled with temperature 0.7. We compute per-dataset directions via difference-in-means, normalize each, and average across the four domains to guard against overfitting R^\hat{R} to a single reasoning task. The final R^ℓ\hat{R}_{\ell} is the unit vector of this average.

Coupling Evidence.

We measure the whitened cosine similarity cosw⁡(R^ℓ,S^ℓ)\cos_{w}(\hat{R}_{\ell},\hat{S}_{\ell}) at every layer. Whitening removes trivial correlations introduced by activation-space anisotropy. In both models, cosw\cos_{w} is consistently negative across the mid-to-deep layers: 3B is negative from L10 onward, and 7B from L4 onward. A negative cosw\cos_{w} means the two directions point in opposing ways, so optimizing along the reasoning direction moves representations away from the safety direction. The absolute magnitude is modest, with mean |cosw|≈0.13|\cos_{w}|\approx 0.13, so most of the reasoning-induced activation change falls outside the safety subspace. The consistent negative sign, however, indicates that reasoning improvements carry a small but systematic cost to safety representations.

3.4 Locating Safety-Specific Layers

The coupling in §3.3 spans many layers, but a practical intervention requires knowing which layers to target. Each transformer layer encodes different aspects of the input; we need to distinguish layers where fine-tuning specifically disrupts safety-relevant representations from layers whose change reflects general instruction-format adaptation. We locate these layers using CKA distance ratios and confirm the result with linear probes.

We measure how much fine-tuning shifts each layer’s hidden states on harmful inputs (HEx-PHI) versus harmless ones (Alpaca) using linear CKA distance. The ratio rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} divides the CKA distance on harmful inputs by that on harmless inputs; a ratio above 1 isolates safety-specific change from general adaptation. The ratio profile reveals a clear peak in both models. rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} peaks in {L20,…,L26}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\} for 3B, reaching 2.27 at L23, where safety-specific change is more than twice the general change. The 7B peak spans {L15,…,L19}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} with rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} ranging from 1.25 to 1.50, meaning safety-specific representational change exceeds general change by 25–50% in these layers. Outside these regions, the ratio either falls below 1, as in 7B {L21,…,L27}\{\text{L21},\ldots,\text{L27}\} where rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} ranges from 0.70 to 0.91, indicating capability-dominant drift, or reflects negligible absolute change in early layers where both distances are near zero.

To verify that the CKA-identified peak layers encode safety-relevant decisions, we train two linear probes at each layer on hidden states from the base model and AM-SFT, as described in Appendix C.4. The harm-perception probe classifies inputs as harmful or harmless using ground-truth labels. The safety-decision probe classifies whether the model will refuse or fulfill the request, using the model’s own behavior as labels. Figure 2 plots the results. The harm-perception probe stays near-perfect after fine-tuning at both scales, reaching 0.98 for 3B and 0.98 for 7B: the model still recognizes harmful requests. The safety-decision probe, by contrast, collapses to the majority-class baseline, the accuracy of always predicting the dominant label, at every layer: the model no longer acts on what it recognizes. RIM is therefore a decision failure, not a perception failure.

Safety-Decision Layers (M1M_{1}). We define M1M_{1} as this contiguous CKA peak: M1={L20,…,L26}M_{1}=\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\} for 3B and M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} for 7B. The probe analysis supports this choice: base-model safety-decision probe accuracy exceeds the majority-class baseline within M1M_{1} in both models, indicating that these layers encode refuse/fulfill decisions before fine-tuning disrupts them. CKA and the safety-decision probe thus converge on the same layers. M1M_{1} is an initial estimate that may be expanded based on post-training displacement diagnostics, with rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 as the expansion boundary.

3.5 Effect of Coupling on Safety Behavior

If the coupling identified in §3.3 is real, reasoning fine-tuning should displace representations along S^\hat{S} in the M1M_{1} layers identified in §3.4.

Measuring Displacement.

We capture this shift directly with per-layer displacement:

dSℓ=(𝐡SFT,ℓ−𝐡base,ℓ)⋅S^ℓ.d_{S_{\ell}}=(\mathbf{h}_{\text{SFT},\ell}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{base},\ell})\cdot\hat{S}_{\ell}.

where 𝐡SFT,ℓ\mathbf{h}_{\text{SFT},\ell} and 𝐡base,ℓ\mathbf{h}_{\text{base},\ell} are the layer-ℓ\ell hidden states from the fine-tuned model and the base model respectively, both recorded at the last non-padding token position. This projects the fine-tuning-induced activation change onto the safety direction. A negative dSd_{S} means the layer moved away from safe behavior; a positive dSd_{S} means it moved toward it.

We measure dSd_{S} on HEx-PHI harmful prompts because safety-relevant displacement is only meaningful on inputs where the model must choose between refusing and fulfilling the request. On benign inputs no such decision is at stake.

Displacement Results.

Figure 3 reports per-layer cosw\cos_{w} and dSd_{S} within M1M_{1}. For 7B, displacement runs uniformly negative with a mean of −7.08-7.08. Negative displacement means the layer’s representations moved away from the safety direction after fine-tuning, consistent with the coupling sign. The 3B pattern differs: displacement is large in magnitude but alternates in sign across layers, with a mean of −0.013-0.013, near zero. Individual layers shift substantially, but the shifts partially cancel across layers. The uniform sign in 7B indicates directionally consistent displacement across layers, whereas the sign-mixed 3B profile indicates heterogeneous layerwise displacement.

Per-Prompt Correlation.

For each HEx-PHI prompt, we compute the mean dSd_{S} across M1M_{1} and the change in GPT-4o-mini harmfulness score between the base model and AM-SFT. The two quantities correlate with Spearman ρ=0.475\rho=0.475 for 3B and ρ=0.277\rho=0.277 for 7B, both statistically significant. Prompts where fine-tuning shifts representations further from the safety direction also show larger safety degradation.

Mechanism Summary.

Under the coupling identified in §3.3, reasoning fine-tuning displaces safety representations in the M1M_{1} layers identified in §3.4. The displacement is systematic, as confirmed by the per-prompt correlation, but differs in sign pattern across scales. Together, these results support a testable representation-space account in which reasoning–safety coupling is associated with collateral displacement. The same analysis also identifies the initial penalty target M1M_{1}.

4 Mitigation Method: Safety-Direction Penalty

This section presents the Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP) and the diagnostic procedure that selects its penalty scope. The coupling analysis reveals that reasoning fine-tuning perturbs safety representations across many layers, with safety-specific change concentrated in the safety-decision layers. The simplest countermeasure is to penalize this shift during training. SDP adds a squared displacement penalty along the safety direction to the fine-tuning loss. A diagnostic targeting procedure then determines which layers receive this penalty. CKA ratios, probes, and displacement profiles together select the penalty scope.

4.1 Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP)

We add a single term to the standard cross-entropy loss: the squared displacement along S^\hat{S}, averaged over a selected layer set MM. We call this the Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP). The SDP training loss is:

ℒ=ℒCE+γs⋅1|M|∑ℓ∈M(dSℓ)2\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}+\gamma_{s}\cdot\frac{1}{|M|}\sum_{\ell\in M}\bigl(d_{S_{\ell}}\bigr)^{2} (1)

where ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} is the standard cross-entropy loss on AM-DeepSeek reasoning data. The scalar γs\gamma_{s} is the penalty weight, MM is the penalty layer set, and dSℓd_{S_{\ell}} is the displacement along the safety direction defined in §3.5.

Geometrically, the penalty acts directly along S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} with strength proportional to the signed displacement; it does not directly penalize orthogonal components. The full gradient derivation and its optimization boundary appear in Appendix D.1.

Two design choices follow from the diagnostics. Squaring makes the penalty sign-invariant, handling the 3B cross-layer sign variability (§3.5). Averaging over |M||M| keeps the per-layer penalty magnitude comparable regardless of how many layers MM contains.

4.2 Diagnostic Targeting Procedure

SDP needs a layer set MM. The diagnostic pipeline from §3 supplies the selection criteria. The targeting procedure has four steps: (1) select initial layers from the CKA peak, (2) apply SDP and evaluate, (3) diagnose displacement compensation if safety does not recover, and (4) expand the penalty scope within the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 boundary if needed.

Initial Layer Selection.

We select the initial penalty scope M1M_{1} as the contiguous rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} peak identified in §3.4: M1={L20,…,L26}M_{1}=\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\} for 3B and M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} for 7B. We then train with the SDP loss (Eq. 1) over M=M1M=M_{1}. For 7B, this initial scope restores safety to base-model level. For 3B, safety does not recover despite M1M_{1} displacement compressing to near zero.

Compensation Diagnostic.

For 7B, the initial scope already restores safety, so no further diagnostic is needed. For 3B, safety does not recover after penalizing M1M_{1}; we measure displacement beyond the penalized layers. Post-M1M_{1} displacement persists at AM-SFT level: suppressing displacement in one layer set leaves the model free to maintain it elsewhere. We call this displacement compensation.

Scope Expansion.

Compensation signals that the initial scope is too narrow. We expand MM to include all contiguous layers satisfying rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1, the boundary where safety-specific representational drift exceeds general drift. For 3B, this yields the expanded scope M={L19,…,L32}M=\{\text{L19},\ldots,\text{L32}\}, spanning 14 layers. Expanding beyond the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 boundary degrades safety, as confirmed by a 7B scope-violation experiment in Appendix D.6.

Procedure Summary.

The procedure stops when the selected scope removes downstream displacement and restores safety, or when the finite contiguous region with rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 has been exhausted. For 7B, the initial scope M={L15,…,L19}M=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} meets the stopping condition. For 3B, displacement compensation after the initial scope triggers expansion to M={L19,…,L32}M=\{\text{L19},\ldots,\text{L32}\}; the procedure does not search outside the diagnostic boundary. If a future setting still fails after exhausting this region, the procedure reports that no successful scope was found.

The loss form (Eq. 1) is unchanged; only MM changes.44 4 Initial application results, compensation analysis, and boundary evidence appear in Appendices D.2–D.4.

After SDP, the per-prompt correlations between displacement and safety degradation are ρ=−0.164\rho=-0.164 for 3B and ρ=−0.119\rho=-0.119 for 7B, neither statistically significant. This result is consistent with SDP reducing the displacement–behavior association identified in §3.5.

5 Results and Analysis

This section reports the evaluation results of SDP and analyzes how RIM and its mitigation manifest in generation behavior. We evaluate SDP with the final penalty scopes determined by the targeting procedure in §4.2: M={L19,…,L32}M=\{\text{L19},\ldots,\text{L32}\}, spanning 14 layers, for 3B and M={L15,…,L19}M=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\}, spanning 5 layers, for 7B. The two scales follow different paths to these scopes: 7B succeeds with the initial M1M_{1} in one step, while 3B requires scope expansion after a compensation diagnostic (details in Appendix D.2–D.4). We first report evaluation metrics, then analyze the generation behavior underlying these results.

5.1 Evaluation Results

Setup.

Both models use γs=0.5\gamma_{s}=0.5 (chosen from a grid search) and LoRA rank 16 applied to all linear layers. 3B trains with LR =5​e-​5=5\text{e-}5 for 3 epochs with batch size 8; 7B trains with LR =2.5​e-​5=2.5\text{e-}5 for 4 epochs with batch size 16.

Safety Recovery.

Table 2 reports the main results. SDP restores safety to base-model level at both scales. For 3B, the HEx-PHI harmfulness rate drops from 20.3% to 10.0%, matching the base model, and SafetyBench accuracy recovers from 57.9% to 69.6%, exceeding the base model’s 69.1%. For 7B, the harmfulness rate drops from 25.3% to 11.3%, below the base model’s 13.3%, and SafetyBench accuracy recovers from 76.5% to 79.4%, matching the base model. Both evaluated safety metrics return to or exceed their base-model values.

Reasoning Preservation.

Reasoning performance remains comparable to the base model. GPQA shows modest decreases: 3.8 pp for 3B and 2.0 pp for 7B relative to the base model. AIME scores are comparable or improved: 7B AIME 2024 rises from 10.4 to 15.0; 3B AIME scores remain within the variance of the base model (Table 2). SDP restores the evaluated safety metrics while retaining most evaluated reasoning performance, with benchmark-specific trade-offs.

5.2 Behavioral Analysis

Detailed response analysis in Appendix E.2 shows that AM-SFT concentrates harm in extended-thinking responses and that SDP restores safety through different behavioral channels at the two scales. SDP reduces conditional harmfulness for 3B but suppresses extended-thinking adoption for 7B.

6 Conclusion

We study when Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM) emerges, how it manifests in representation space, and how it can be mitigated. Across the evaluated architectures, model scales, and reasoning datasets, RIM does not emerge in every model–dataset–training setting, supporting a conditional rather than universal characterization. In settings that satisfy our operational RIM criterion, reasoning–safety coupling and displacement along the safety direction are consistently associated with behavioral safety degradation. CKA ratios and linear probes locate a compact set of safety-decision layers where the model continues to recognize harmful requests but no longer reliably refuses them. These diagnostics motivate the Safety-Direction Penalty (SDP) and guide its layer scope: the initial scope is retained when it restores safety, whereas residual displacement motivates expansion within the diagnostic boundary. Under the evaluated RIM settings, SDP restores safety to base-model levels while retaining most evaluated reasoning performance, without safety training data, a reference policy, or inference-time intervention.

Limitations

The evidence supports RIM as a conditional failure mode of reasoning fine-tuning under the evaluated conditions. Our positive RIM and SDP results focus on Qwen2.5-Instruct, while the MetaMathQA, Gemma, Ministral, and Qwen2.5-14B checks provide initial evidence across datasets, model families, and scales. Broader controlled studies could further characterize how corpus, architecture, and scale affect the emergence of RIM. SDP currently estimates one fixed-template refusal–compliance direction per layer at the last-token representation. Future work could examine more diverse refusal responses, multidimensional safety subspaces, and intermediate reasoning representations. We interpret the geometric analysis as a local account of SDP’s intervention rather than a general causal characterization of model safety. Matched comparisons with external fine-tuning defenses and further study of targeting efficiency across models would also help contextualize SDP’s benefits and costs.

Ethical Considerations

This work aims to improve the safety of fine-tuned language models by diagnosing and mitigating Reasoning-Induced Misalignment. The diagnostic pipeline identifies which layers are most vulnerable to safety degradation, and the safety direction extraction reveals the geometric structure of refusal behavior. This information could in principle be misused to target safety-vulnerable layers for adversarial attacks or to remove safety behavior more efficiently. We believe the defensive value outweighs this risk: understanding why safety degrades is a prerequisite for building robust mitigations, and the safety direction extraction method builds on publicly available techniques (Arditi et al., 2024). The HEx-PHI benchmark used for evaluation contains harmful prompts by design; we use it strictly for safety evaluation and do not release model outputs on these prompts. All experiments use publicly available models and datasets; no new harmful content is generated or distributed. We used Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) to assist with prose editing, code development, and experimental analysis. All hypotheses, methodological decisions, and scientific conclusions are the authors’ own.

Appendix A Experimental Setup

This section describes the models, training procedures, and datasets used in all experiments.

A.1 Models

We use the Qwen2.5-Instruct family (Qwen et al., 2025) at three scales: 3B and 7B are the primary RIM and SDP evaluation targets, while 14B provides a within-family scale check (Appendix E.1). These models have undergone instruction tuning and safety alignment during post-training, making them a suitable testbed for studying how reasoning fine-tuning can degrade existing safety guardrails. Table 3 summarizes the architecture at each scale.

For the model-family scope checks, we use Gemma 3 4B IT (Gemma Team, 2025) and Ministral 3 3B Instruct (Liu et al., 2026). Gemma is trained and evaluated in a text-only setting, with LoRA restricted to the text decoder and the vision tower excluded. For Ministral, both the base evaluation and AM-SFT training use the official BF16 checkpoint.

A.2 Training Datasets

For the primary Qwen2.5-3B/7B experiments, we use the first 10,000 examples from AM-DeepSeek (Zhao et al., 2025), a distilled reasoning corpus.

Composition.

Categories are assigned by keyword matching and are not mutually exclusive (20.5% of examples match both math and code keywords):

  • •

    Math: 5,498 examples (55.0%).

  • •

    Code: 3,138 examples (31.4%).

  • •

    General reasoning: 3,416 examples (34.2%).

Format.

Each example consists of a single-turn conversation: one user query and one assistant response containing an extended thinking trace enclosed in <think>...</think> tags followed by a final answer. All 10,000 examples contain <think> tags. Mean output length is 2,408 tokens (median 1,572; range 202–25,127) measured with the Qwen2.5 tokenizer.

Safety content.

The dataset contains no harmful content. Keyword screening flags 146 examples (1.5%), nearly all involving the term “ricin” in chemistry or science reasoning contexts rather than harmful instructions.

MetaMathQA control.

For the cross-dataset check, we draw a random 10,000-example subset of MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024) with seed 3407. MetaMathQA provides natural-language step-by-step mathematical solutions. In the sampled subset, none of the 10,000 outputs contains a literal <think> tag. This control changes both corpus identity and the explicit tag convention; it does not isolate response length, mathematical domain, or every other reasoning-format factor.

A.3 Fine-Tuning Configurations

Training configuration.

All fine-tuning uses LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) applied to all linear layers (q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projections). AM-SFT and SDP share the same hyperparameters; the only difference is that AM-SFT sets the penalty weight γs=0\gamma_{s}=0 while SDP uses γs=0.5\gamma_{s}=0.5. Table 4 reports the full configuration for 3B and 7B. Intermediate SDP configurations (penalty scope M={L20,…,L26}M=\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\} and M={L20,L21}M=\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\}) use the same hyperparameters as the final 3B SDP but with narrower penalty scope.

14B AM-SFT configuration.

We trained two independent AM-SFT runs on 14B-Instruct with different hyperparameters; neither reproduced RIM. Both use LoRA with r=16r=16, α=16\alpha=16, targeting all linear layers, with max sequence length 16,384. Table 5 reports the configurations.

Table 6 records the executed settings for the additional scope checks. The Qwen2.5-3B MetaMathQA run is a matched corpus substitution relative to the 10,000-example Qwen AM-DeepSeek setup. Gemma and Ministral use 24,337 AM-DeepSeek examples under their documented model-specific settings, so these runs test additional model families but are not architecture-only controlled comparisons.

This section describes the safety and reasoning benchmarks used throughout the paper. All model inference uses vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) with greedy decoding (temperature 0) unless otherwise noted.

A.4 Scope-Check Evaluation Results

We use the same operational criterion throughout: RIM requires safety degradation after benign reasoning SFT while evaluated reasoning performance is preserved or improved. The experiments below test whether this conjunction appears under an additional reasoning corpus, two additional model families, and a larger within-family scale. They are induction-scope checks; SDP is evaluated only after a setting meets the RIM criterion.

MetaMathQA-SFT does not meet the RIM criterion because its evaluated reasoning endpoints are below the submitted Qwen2.5-3B base values. For Gemma, HEx-PHI harmfulness improves from 12.67% to 5.00%, while SafetyBench and both AIME endpoints decline; the required safety-degradation-plus-reasoning-preservation conjunction is therefore absent. For Ministral, HEx-PHI also does not worsen, while SafetyBench, GPQA, and AIME decline substantially; this setting likewise does not enter the operational RIM regime. The two Qwen2.5-14B runs also fail the criterion because neither degrades safety relative to the base model. Because none of these additional settings exhibits RIM, SDP is not applied to them.

For Ministral, both the base evaluation and AM-SFT training use the official BF16 checkpoint mistralai/Ministral-3-3B-Instruct-2512-BF16. After dynamic-LoRA loading failed, AM-SFT evaluation used the merged adapter under vLLM 0.13. We therefore report Ministral as a descriptive cross-architecture scope check, not as a matched causal architecture-only comparison.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocols

B.1 Safety Evaluation

We evaluate safety with two complementary benchmarks: HEx-PHI for open-ended harmful-response detection and SafetyBench for multiple-choice safety knowledge.

HEx-PHI.

We use the HEx-PHI benchmark (Qi et al., 2024), which contains 300 harmful prompts spanning 10 categories: Illegal Activity, Hate/Harassment/Violence, Malware, Physical Harm, Economic Harm, Fraud/Deception, Adult Content, Political Campaigning, Privacy Violation, and Tailored Financial Advice. One category is excluded due to systematic judge failures. We adopt the evaluation protocol of Yan et al. (2026).

Generation.

Each prompt is passed to the model with max_tokens = 16,384 and temperature = 0. For models that produce thinking tokens (enclosed in <think>...</think>), we report both strip-think results (thinking tokens removed before judging) and think-inclusive results (full output judged).

Judge.

We use GPT-4o-mini as the judge model. The judge receives the harmful prompt and the model’s response. It classifies the response as either refuse (the model declines the harmful request) or fulfill (the model provides the requested harmful content). A response scoring 3 or higher on the 5-point harmfulness scale is classified as fulfill. The HEx-PHI misalignment rate is the percentage of prompts classified as fulfill.

Judge prompt.

No system prompt is used; the entire prompt is sent as a single user message. The thinking trace is stripped before judging: the judge evaluates only the user-visible output after <think> removal.

Judge details.

Model: GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI unversioned alias). Temperature: 0.0. Each prompt is judged once (no majority vote). Greedy decoding (temperature 0) makes model generation deterministic, so the primary source of evaluation variance is the GPT-4o-mini judge. To quantify this noise, we re-judged three configurations (3B AM-SFT, 3B SDP, 7B AM-SFT) five times each with the same judge and parameters. The standard deviation of the misalignment rate across six judgings (one original plus five re-runs) is 0.35 to 0.52 pp, with a maximum range of 1.3 pp. Only 4 to 5 of 300 prompts change verdict across six judgings, confirming that judge noise does not affect our conclusions.

SafetyBench.

SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024) is a multiple-choice benchmark for safety knowledge. We use the full English subset (11,435 questions across 7 categories) and report accuracy (percentage of correct answers). Missing predictions are counted as incorrect.

The prompt is wrapped in the model’s chat template as a single user message with no system prompt (zero-shot). Generation uses greedy decoding (temperature 0, max_new_tokens = 16). Options are labeled with 0-indexed integers, not letters. The answer is extracted from the generated text by regex: we take the first integer in the output and check whether it falls within the valid option range. If integer extraction fails, we fall back to letter matching (A→\to0, B→\to1, …) and then to case-insensitive substring matching against option text. Empty responses trigger up to 3 retries.

B.2 Reasoning Evaluation

We evaluate reasoning with AIME for mathematical competition problems and GPQA for graduate-level science questions.

AIME.

AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) is a high-school mathematics competition known for problems that require extended multi-step reasoning. We evaluate on AIME 2024 (Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2024) (30 problems) and AIME 2025 (Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2025) (30 problems). Each configuration is run 8 times; we report mean ±\pm standard deviation.

Each problem is prompted as a single user message (no system prompt) with the suffix: “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.”

Generation parameters.

Temperature =0.7=0.7, top-p=0.8p=0.8, top-k=20k=20, repetition penalty =1.05=1.05, min tokens =50=50, max tokens =16,384=16{,}384.

Answer extraction.

We use a multi-stage regex cascade. First, we extract \boxed{…} with nested brace matching. If that fails, we fall back to <answer> tags, “the answer is” patterns, #### delimiters, or LaTeX delimiters. If no \boxed{} is found or the output is shorter than 800 characters, the model retries up to 3 times. Final correctness is determined by numerical equivalence via the HuggingFace math-verify library.

Multiple runs.

The 8 AIME runs are independent vLLM processes with temperature 0.7. No per-request sampling seed is set in SamplingParams, so run-to-run variation arises from non-deterministic asynchronous batched decoding in vLLM, not from explicit seed changes. A random.seed(3407) is set in the evaluation harness, but it only affects Python’s standard random module, which is not called during generation or evaluation.

GPQA.

GPQA (Rein et al., 2024) contains graduate-level science questions across physics, chemistry, and biology. We use the GPQA Main full set (448 questions) and report accuracy from a single run. Unlike AIME, we do not run GPQA multiple times, so no error bar is reported.

Each question is prompted as a single user message (no system prompt) with the same suffix as AIME: “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.” Answer options (A/B/C/D) are embedded in the question text. Generation parameters match AIME: temperature =0.7=0.7, top-p=0.8p=0.8, top-k=20k=20, repetition penalty =1.05=1.05, max tokens =16,384=16{,}384. GPQA has no retry mechanism (unlike AIME).

Answers are extracted by parsing the generation for the option letter. We check, in order: normalized exact match against the gold letter, prefix patterns (e.g., “B:”, “B.”), regex patterns (e.g., “option B”, “(B)”, “\boxed{B}”), and normalized exact match against the gold option content.

Appendix C Diagnostic Methods

This section details the diagnostic tools used to identify and characterize the reasoning-safety coupling described in the main text.

C.1 Safety and Reasoning Direction Extraction

Adapting the difference-in-means framework of Arditi et al. (2024), we extract the safety direction S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} at each layer. Arditi et al. contrast harmful versus harmless inputs to find a direction encoding harm recognition. We instead contrast refusal versus compliance responses to the same harmful prompt, isolating the refuse/comply decision rather than input harmfulness. We use 520 harmful prompts from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023). For each prompt, we construct two conversations: one with a templated refusal response and one with the AdvBench compliance target.

Refusal template.

The refusal response uses the following fixed template:

Using one fixed refusal response holds response style constant across prompts and reduces nuisance variation in the difference-in-means estimate. This control also narrows the construct: S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} captures the refuse/comply contrast induced by this template and may not span natural refusal diversity or a multidimensional safety subspace. We run both conversations through the base model and record hidden states at the last non-padding token of the full sequence (prompt and response). The raw safety direction at layer ℓ\ell is:

𝐬ℓ=1520​∑i=1520(𝐡refuse,ℓ(i)−𝐡comply,ℓ(i))\mathbf{s}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{520}\sum_{i=1}^{520}\bigl(\mathbf{h}_{\text{refuse},\ell}^{(i)}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{comply},\ell}^{(i)}\bigr)

The unit safety direction is S^ℓ=𝐬ℓ/‖𝐬ℓ‖\hat{S}_{\ell}=\mathbf{s}_{\ell}/\|\mathbf{s}_{\ell}\|.

The reasoning direction R^ℓ\hat{R}_{\ell} is extracted from four reasoning benchmarks spanning competition mathematics and graduate-level science. For each problem, we contrast the base model’s hidden states when processing a correct (reference) solution versus the base model’s own incorrect generation. We record hidden states at the last non-padding token of the full conversation (question and response), using left truncation with a maximum length of 8,192 tokens. Incorrect generations use temperature =0.7=0.7, top-p=0.8p=0.8, top-k=20k=20, repetition penalty =1.05=1.05, max tokens =16,384=16{,}384.

Datasets for R^\hat{R} extraction.

We use four datasets:

  1. 1.

    AIME/Putnam competition pool (356 problems). A mixed pool of AIME 2022–2025 problems (approximately 120) and Putnam competition problems (approximately 236) from Putnam-AXIOM (Gulati et al., 2025). Correct solutions come from official competition solutions.

  2. 2.

    GPQA Main (Rein et al., 2024) (448 questions). Graduate-level science questions across physics, chemistry, and biology. Correct solutions come from the expert explanation field in the GPQA dataset.

  3. 3.

    MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024) (499 problems after filtering). A 500-problem subset of the MATH benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2021) spanning algebra, geometry, number theory, precalculus, and probability. One problem with a solution shorter than 50 characters is excluded during preprocessing.

  4. 4.

    OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024) (906 problems). Text-only, open-ended competition problems from mathematics and physics olympiads. Problems containing images are excluded.

Filtering and aggregation.

We filter contrast pairs to ensure minimum quality: reference solutions must be at least 50 characters and model outputs at least 10 characters; truncated outputs are excluded. Per-dataset sample counts (correct / incorrect) for 3B: AIME/Putnam (38 / 316), GPQA (133 / 315), MATH-500 (313 / 185), OlympiadBench (189 / 704). For 7B: AIME/Putnam (54 / 301), GPQA (149 / 299), MATH-500 (358 / 141), OlympiadBench (275 / 629). Per-dataset directions are computed via difference-in-means and normalized; the final R^ℓ\hat{R}_{\ell} is the unit vector of the average across the four per-dataset directions.

Tables 8 and 9 report the full per-layer whitened cosine similarity cosw⁡(R^ℓ,S^ℓ)\cos_{w}(\hat{R}_{\ell},\hat{S}_{\ell}) profiles.

C.2 Whitening Procedure

The whitened cosine similarity removes trivial correlations caused by activation-space anisotropy. We use Mahalanobis whitening (equivalent to ZCA whitening implemented via matrix solve rather than explicit eigendecomposition).

At each layer ℓ\ell, we compute the covariance matrix Σℓ\Sigma_{\ell} from 600 base-model hidden states (300 HEx-PHI + 300 Alpaca-Cleaned prompts) at the last non-padding token position. We apply ridge regularization: Σreg=Σℓ+10−3⋅𝐈\Sigma_{\text{reg}}=\Sigma_{\ell}+10^{-3}\cdot\mathbf{I}. The whitened cosine similarity is:

cosw⁡(R^,S^)=R^⊤​Σreg−1​S^(R^⊤​Σreg−1​R^)⋅(S^⊤​Σreg−1​S^)\cos_{w}(\hat{R},\hat{S})=\frac{\hat{R}^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}\hat{S}}{\sqrt{(\hat{R}^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}\hat{R})\cdot(\hat{S}^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}\hat{S})}}

Each layer uses its own covariance matrix (per-layer whitening). The effective condition number of Σreg\Sigma_{\text{reg}} remains below 4×1054\times 10^{5} at all layers, ensuring numerical stability.

C.3 CKA Computation

We use linear Centered Kernel Alignment (Kornblith et al., 2019) to measure representational similarity between the base model and AM-SFT. At layer ℓ\ell, let 𝐗∈ℝn×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be the base hidden-state matrix. Let 𝐘∈ℝn×d\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be the AM-SFT hidden-state matrix. Here, nn is the number of prompts and dd is the hidden dimension. Both matrices are mean-centered before computation: 𝐗←𝐗−𝐗¯\mathbf{X}\leftarrow\mathbf{X}-\bar{\mathbf{X}}, 𝐘←𝐘−𝐘¯\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow\mathbf{Y}-\bar{\mathbf{Y}}. Linear CKA is:

CKA​(𝐗,𝐘)=‖𝐘⊤​𝐗‖F2‖𝐗⊤​𝐗‖F​‖𝐘⊤​𝐘‖F\text{CKA}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})=\frac{\|\mathbf{Y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}\;\|\mathbf{Y}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}\|_{F}}

We compute 1−CKA1-\text{CKA} as the CKA distance (higher = more representational drift). The ratio rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} divides the CKA distance on harmful prompts (300 HEx-PHI) by the CKA distance on harmless prompts (300 Alpaca-Cleaned (Taori et al., 2023)).

rCKA=1−CKAh1−CKAa.r_{\mathrm{CKA}}=\frac{1-\mathrm{CKA}_{h}}{1-\mathrm{CKA}_{a}}.

A ratio >1>1 means safety-specific drift exceeds instruction-format drift; a ratio <1<1 means the layer’s drift is dominated by instruction-format adaptation. All hidden states are read at the last non-padding token position.

Tables 10 and 11 report the full per-layer CKA profiles. Both models show a clear rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} peak in the mid-to-deep layers that defines M1M_{1} (§3.4). For 3B, early layers ({L2,…,L11}\{\text{L2},\ldots,\text{L11}\}) also show high ratios (1.20–2.21) but with negligible absolute CKA distance (<0.035<0.035), reflecting noise rather than meaningful safety-specific change. The {L12,…,L16}\{\text{L12},\ldots,\text{L16}\} valley (rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} = 0.85–0.95) separates this noise region from the M1M_{1} peak at {L20,…,L26}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\} (1.45–2.27). Beyond M1M_{1}, the ratio gradually declines toward 1.0 ({L33,…,L35}\{\text{L33},\ldots,\text{L35}\}: 1.02–1.05). For 7B, the M1M_{1} peak at {L15,…,L19}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} (1.25–1.50) is flanked by a sharp drop. L20 is borderline (1.09), and {L21,…,L27}\{\text{L21},\ldots,\text{L27}\} fall below 1 (0.70–0.91). This indicates that drift in these deeper layers is capability-dominant rather than safety-specific.

C.4 Probe Training Details

Harm-perception probe.

We combine 300 HEx-PHI harmful prompts with 300 Alpaca-Cleaned (Taori et al., 2023) harmless prompts (600 total). The 300 HEx-PHI prompts are the full set (10 categories, 30 prompts each, no sampling). The 300 Alpaca prompts are drawn from the 51,760-prompt Alpaca-Cleaned corpus using a deterministic sample with seed 42.55 5 random.Random(42).sample(all_prompts, 300) The same 600 prompts are reused across all diagnostic experiments (probing, CKA, whitening covariance) and across both model scales, enforced by an assertion check. This fixed seed ensures that all reported numbers are reproducible. Labels are ground-truth: harmful = 1, harmless = 0. Each prompt is formatted with the model’s chat template and passed through the model in a single forward pass. We extract the hidden state at the last non-padding token position at every layer, yielding a matrix of shape [600,d][600,d] per layer (3B: d=2048d=2048; 7B: d=3584d=3584). We train a logistic regression classifier with 5-fold cross-validation (sklearn LogisticRegressionCV, L2L_{2} penalty, lbfgs solver) and report the mean accuracy across folds. We repeat this independently for the base model and AM-SFT.

Harm-perception probe accuracy is near-perfect at both scales: 3B base 0.981 / AM-SFT 0.983; 7B base 0.983 / AM-SFT 0.986. RIM does not impair the model’s ability to recognize harmful requests.

Safety-decision probe.

We use only the 300 HEx-PHI harmful prompts. Labels are the model’s own behavior: each prompt is passed to the model for generation (max_tokens = 4,096, temperature = 0). GPT-4o-mini judges each response as either refuse (0) or fulfill (1). We run this process separately for the base model and AM-SFT, producing independent label sets.

Label distributions for the base model: 3B ≈\approx 274 refuse / 26 fulfill; 7B ≈\approx 259 refuse / 41 fulfill. The majority-class baseline (fraction of the dominant class) is therefore ≈\approx91% (3B) and ≈\approx86% (7B); above-baseline accuracy indicates that the layer encodes decision-relevant information beyond class imbalance.

Hidden states are extracted from the same forward pass as the harm-perception probe (restricted to the 300 HEx-PHI prompts). A logistic regression classifier is trained per layer with 5-fold cross-validation, independently for base and AM-SFT.

Position selection.

Both probes read hidden states at the last non-padding token, where the model’s next-token prediction determines whether generation begins with a refusal or a compliance. Appendix C.5 reports results at the mean-pooled position; qualitative conclusions are identical.

C.5 Position Analysis

All main-text results measure displacement and probe accuracy at the last non-padding token position (position (a)). We also computed all diagnostics at the prompt-encoding last-token position (position (b)), i.e., the last token after encoding the prompt alone. The qualitative conclusions are identical: the safety-decision probe collapses in the same layers, dSd_{S} displacement concentrates in M1M_{1}, and per-prompt ρ\rho remains significant. Position (a) yields slightly higher ρ\rho values, consistent with the hypothesis that the last token is where the refuse/fulfill decision concentrates.

C.6 Per-Prompt Displacement Correlation

This subsection details the per-prompt correlation between displacement along the safety direction and behavioral safety degradation, validating the link between the geometric diagnostic and model behavior.

Per-prompt correlation details.

We measure the signed mean dSd_{S} across M1M_{1} at the prompt-encoding position, without taking the absolute value, so that the correlation captures the direction of the shift. We correlate this with the per-prompt change in GPT-4o-mini harmfulness score.

For the AM-SFT correlation, the score change is computed between the base model and AM-SFT. We restrict the analysis to prompts whose score changes after fine-tuning, yielding N=99N=99 for 3B and N=97N=97 for 7B out of 300 HEx-PHI prompts. Spearman ρ\rho is 0.4750.475 with p=6.7×10−7p=6.7\times 10^{-7} for 3B and 0.2770.277 with p=0.006p=0.006 for 7B.

For the SDP correlation severance, the score change is computed between the base model and the SDP model. The nonzero-change subset yields N=93N=93 for 3B and N=68N=68 for 7B. ρ\rho drops to −0.164-0.164 with p=0.116p=0.116 for 3B and −0.119-0.119 with p=0.335p=0.335 for 7B, both non-significant.

Appendix D Layer Refinement and Ablation

This section presents the layer refinement experiments that determine the final penalty scope for each model scale, followed by ablation studies validating the design choices.

D.1 Geometric Effect of the SDP Penalty

Let Δ​𝐡ℓ=𝐡SFT,ℓ−𝐡base,ℓ\Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}=\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{SFT},\ell}-\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{base},\ell}, so dSℓ=Δ​𝐡ℓ⊤​S^ℓd_{S_{\ell}}=\Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\top}\hat{S}_{\ell}. The direct gradient of the layerwise penalty is

∇Δ​𝐡ℓγs|M|​(dSℓ)2=2​γs|M|​(Δ​𝐡ℓ⊤​S^ℓ)​S^ℓ.\nabla_{\Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}}\frac{\gamma_{s}}{|M|}(d_{S_{\ell}})^{2}=\frac{2\gamma_{s}}{|M|}(\Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\top}\hat{S}_{\ell})\hat{S}_{\ell}.

Thus the direct constraint acts along S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} and scales with the signed projection magnitude; components orthogonal to S^ℓ\hat{S}_{\ell} are not directly penalized. Because layers share model parameters, updates can couple directions and layers, so this is a local geometric account of the regularizer rather than a complete optimization or causal theorem.

D.2 Initial Application to M1M_{1}

We apply SDP to the initial M1M_{1} at both scales with γs=0.5\gamma_{s}=0.5 (chosen from a grid search; full training configuration in Appendix A.3). Table 12 reports the results.

For 7B (M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\}), SDP restores safety to base-model level: HEx-PHI drops from 25.33% to 11.33% and SafetyBench recovers to 79.44% (base: 79.50%). By contrast, 3B (M1={L20,…,L26}M_{1}=\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\}) does not recover: HEx-PHI drops only marginally to 18.67% (AM-SFT: 20.33%, base: 10.00%). Why the initial 3B application does not recover safety while 7B succeeds requires further analysis. Applying SDP to M1M_{1} suffices for 7B; 3B requires scope expansion beyond M1M_{1}, as detailed in Appendix D.3.

D.3 Compensation beyond M1M_{1}

Both models compress M1M_{1} displacement to near zero, so the penalty reaches its geometric target in both cases. Examining displacement beyond M1M_{1} reveals why the behavioral outcomes diverge: 3B exhibits a compensation effect in the deeper layers. We therefore keep the same SDP loss and refine only the layer set MM. This subsection isolates the compensation effect. The next subsection uses it to choose the expansion boundary, and §5 reports the final evaluation.

Displacement Compensation in 3B and 7B.

In 3B, post-M1M_{1} displacement ({L27,…,L35}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L35}\}) remains at −3.006-3.006 after SDP({L20,…,L26}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\}), comparable to AM-SFT (−2.805-2.805): suppressing M1M_{1} does not reduce downstream displacement. The 7B pattern is opposite: post-M1M_{1} displacement ({L20,…,L24}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L24}\}) collapses from −15.91-15.91 (AM-SFT) to −0.09-0.09 after SDP({L15,…,L19}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\}), a 99% reduction. We call this displacement compensation: suppressing displacement in one layer set leaves the model free to maintain or amplify displacement elsewhere.

Detailed Compensation Analysis (3B).

We report per-layer dSd_{S} values with sign to characterize displacement direction. For magnitude ratios, we use mean |dS||d_{S}| to avoid sign-cancellation artifacts. Table 13 and Figure 4 break down the 3B compensation pattern. Figure 4 plots per-layer dSd_{S} across all 36 layers for four configurations. AM-SFT displacement concentrates in the deep layers (L20+). SDP({L20,…,L26}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\}) suppresses M1M_{1} but leaves the post-M1M_{1} profile intact. SDP({L19,…,L32}\{\text{L19},\ldots,\text{L32}\}) flattens the entire active zone. A narrower ablation SDP({L20,L21}\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\}) isolates the effect: restricting the penalty to two layers amplifies mean |dS||d_{S}| 2.8×\times in the adjacent unpunished layers {L22,…,L26}\{\text{L22},\ldots,\text{L26}\} (Table 13). Compensation occurs wherever the penalty does not reach, whether downstream or within adjacent layers.

Why the Models Differ.

The asymmetry traces to displacement structure. 7B displacement runs uniformly negative from M1M_{1} through all deeper layers: M1M_{1} is the sole source, and constraining it removes the downstream signal. In 3B, post-M1M_{1} displacement is sign-mixed (positive in {L27,…,L31}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L31}\}, negative in {L32,…,L35}\{\text{L32},\ldots,\text{L35}\}), mirroring the sign variability within M1M_{1}. Post-M1M_{1} mean |dS||d_{S}| is 12×\times larger than M1M_{1} mean |dS||d_{S}| (5.68 vs. 0.47), compared to approximately 2×\times for 7B. The 3B post-M1M_{1} displacement operates independently and must be addressed directly.

D.4 Where to Expand: Evidence and Limits

Compensation signals that the initial penalty scope is too narrow for 3B. Before expanding, we verify that the deeper layers are genuinely safety-relevant and identify how far to extend.

Evidence for Expanding to {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\}.

rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} in {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\} ranges from 1.09 to 1.22 (Table 10). Representational drift on harmful inputs exceeds drift on harmless inputs by 9–22%, indicating that these layers remain safety-dominant rather than capability-dominant.

AM-SFT displacement in {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\} is already large before any penalty: signed dSd_{S} ranges from −2.25-2.25 to +3.19+3.19 with mean |dS|=2.53|d_{S}|=2.53 (Figure 4). This displacement persists unchanged after SDP({L20,…,L26}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\}) compresses initial M1M_{1} to near zero (§D.3).

R–S geometric coupling is stronger in {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\} than in initial M1M_{1}: whitened cos⁡(R^,S^)\cos(\hat{R},\hat{S}) ranges from −0.16-0.16 to −0.23-0.23 (mean −0.20-0.20). This exceeds the initial M1M_{1} mean of −0.13-0.13 in magnitude. Safety-dominant CKA ratios, large pre-existing displacement, and stronger R–S coupling together support extending penalty coverage to {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\}.

Evidence for Including L19.

Base-model safety-decision probe accuracy first exceeds the majority-class baseline (0.917) at L18 (0.923), the boundary layer where decision encoding begins (Figure 2). Following our convention of excluding boundary layers, we start the expansion at L19, where the signal is established and rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} is higher. rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} at L19 is 1.49 (Table 10), higher than L26 (1.45), the weakest layer in initial M1M_{1}. It also exceeds every layer in the {L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\} expansion zone (1.09–1.22). Decision encoding and safety-dominant drift both place L19 inside the penalty scope.

Exclusion of {L33,…,L35}\{\text{L33},\ldots,\text{L35}\}.

rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} at {L33,…,L35}\{\text{L33},\ldots,\text{L35}\} ranges from 1.02 to 1.05 (Table 10), indistinguishable from 1. Representational drift in these layers distributes equally across harmful and harmless inputs, with no safety-specific signal. Figure 4 shows large-magnitude dSd_{S} at {L34,L35}\{\text{L34},\text{L35}\}, but this reflects activation scale growth in the final layers rather than safety-relevant displacement. We exclude these layers.

Combining the upward expansion ({L27,…,L32}\{\text{L27},\ldots,\text{L32}\}) and the downward extension (L19), we set the expanded 3B penalty scope M={L19,…,L32}M=\{\text{L19},\ldots,\text{L32}\}, spanning 14 layers. Every included layer satisfies rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1.

Expansion Limits.

For 7B, no expansion is needed: suppressing M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} already eliminates downstream displacement. To test whether the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 boundary constrains expansion, we train a second 7B configuration with the penalty scope expanded from M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} to M={L15,…,L23}M=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L23}\}. The four additional layers include L20 (rCKA=1.09r_{\mathrm{CKA}}=1.09, borderline) and {L21,…,L23}\{\text{L21},\ldots,\text{L23}\} (rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} = 0.74–0.91, capability-dominant).

Boundary Violation Results.

HEx-PHI worsens from 11.33% to 19.33% (+8.0+8.0 pp), nearly reverting to AM-SFT level (25.33%), while SafetyBench and GPQA remain comparable; full results appear in Appendix D.6. The first unpenalized layer, L24, intensifies from −2.66-2.66 to −5.90-5.90, indicating that penalizing capability-dominant layers triggers the same compensation pattern observed in 3B. Expanding within the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 boundary succeeds (3B); expanding beyond it fails (7B).

D.5 SDP({L20,L21}\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\}) Details

The SDP({L20,L21}\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\}) configuration penalizes only {L20,L21}\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\} (2 layers), a strict subset of the initial M1={L20,…,L26}M_{1}=\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L26}\}. It serves as a controlled comparison to test whether a smaller penalty scope triggers stronger compensation.

Results: HEx-PHI = 14.33%, SafetyBench = 46.01%, GPQA = 25.00%, AIME 2024 = 2.5±\pm2.8%, AIME 2025 = 3.8±\pm2.6%. SafetyBench drops sharply (−23.10-23.10 pp from base), indicating that overly narrow penalty scope degrades both safety and general knowledge. The sub-region analysis in §D.3 shows that SDP({L20,L21}\{\text{L20},\text{L21}\}) triggers 2.8×\times mean |dS||d_{S}| amplification in the adjacent unpunished layers {L22,…,L26}\{\text{L22},\ldots,\text{L26}\}.

D.6 7B Scope Ablation

To test the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 expansion boundary (§D.4), we train a 7B SDP configuration with the penalty scope expanded from M1={L15,…,L19}M_{1}=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} to M={L15,…,L23}M=\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L23}\}. The additional layers {L20,…,L23}\{\text{L20},\ldots,\text{L23}\} have rCKAr_{\mathrm{CKA}} values of 1.09, 0.91, 0.79, and 0.74 respectively; {L21,…,L23}\{\text{L21},\ldots,\text{L23}\} are capability-dominant (<1<1). All other hyperparameters match the {L15,…,L19}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\} configuration, as specified in Appendix A.3.

As shown in Table 14, expanding to {L15,…,L23}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L23}\} raises HEx-PHI by +8.0+8.0 pp (from 11.33% to 19.33%), nearly reverting to AM-SFT level (25.33%).

The per-region displacement (Table 15) indicates that penalizing capability-dominant layers (rCKA<1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}<1) constrains normal adaptation, forcing the model to compensate through deeper layers. This suggests that the rCKA>1r_{\mathrm{CKA}}>1 boundary has functional significance beyond a statistical threshold.

D.8 Penalty Computation and Cross-Distribution Transfer

This subsection documents how the penalty is computed during training and why the constraint transfers across input distributions.

SDP computes the penalty exclusively on AM-DeepSeek reasoning examples. HEx-PHI serves for evaluation and diagnostic analysis, never for training. We use the contrastive safety set from AdvBench only to extract the safety direction S^\hat{S} before training begins; no safety examples enter the fine-tuning loss. During each training step, we run the same input through both the current model with the LoRA adapter active and a frozen copy with the adapter disabled. The displacement dSℓd_{S_{\ell}} measures the difference between these two forward passes projected onto S^\hat{S}, isolating the adapter’s effect on the safety direction.

LoRA adapter weights are input-independent: the same weight perturbation Δ​W\Delta W applies to every forward pass regardless of input content. Constraining the adapter’s effect on the safety direction during training therefore constrains it on all inputs, including the held-out HEx-PHI evaluation set.

Appendix E Additional Analysis

This section provides supplementary analysis that extends the main experimental results.

E.1 14B Analysis

Safety-decision probe analysis.

Base model: 279 refuse / 21 fulfill (majority baseline = 0.93). Safety-decision probe accuracy above baseline from L17 onward, peak 0.95 at L30. AM-SFT: 280 refuse / 20 fulfill (baseline = 0.933). Safety-decision probe accuracy increases after AM-SFT, peak 0.97 at {L38,…,L43}\{\text{L38},\ldots,\text{L43}\}. Decision encoding is not disrupted. This contrasts with 3B and 7B, where the same probe collapses to the majority-class baseline after AM-SFT (§3.4).

Extended thinking adoption.

Unlike 3B and 7B, 14B almost never enters <think> mode after AM-DeepSeek training. Table 18 reports the <think> adoption rate across all benchmarks and checkpoints. Without extended thinking, the reasoning-mediated harm channel identified in §5.2 does not activate, consistent with the absence of safety degradation.

E.2 Behavioral Analysis

Beyond the evaluation results above, we trace how reasoning behavior is associated with RIM and how SDP intervenes through different channels at 3B and 7B.

Extended Thinking Mediates Safety Degradation.

Base models never produce <think> tags; after AM-SFT, adoption reaches 46% for 3B and 60% for 7B. Among responses that use <think>, 41.7% are harmful for 3B and 39.2% for 7B. Among responses without <think>, only 1.9% and 4.2% are harmful respectively, a 9–22×\times gap. Responses that enter extended thinking are far more likely to produce harmful content than those that do not. Reasoning fine-tuning degrades safety primarily through responses where it activates extended thinking.

Among the harmful <think> responses, 67% explicitly mention safety or ethics concerns in the thinking trace. Over 90% frame the response as helping the user, across N=58N=58 harmful think responses for 3B and N=71N=71 for 7B. The model recognizes harm during reasoning but overrides the safety boundary, supporting the probe finding in §3.4: RIM is a decision failure, not a perception failure.

Behavioral Channels of SDP.

We decompose HEx-PHI responses along two axes: <think> adoption rate and conditional harmful rate, defined as the fraction of <think>-using responses judged harmful. Table 19 reports both metrics.

SDP operates through opposite channels at the two scales. 3B SDP preserves extended-thinking behavior: <think> adoption rises from 46% to 100%, but the conditional harm rate drops from 42% to 10%. 7B SDP suppresses extended-thinking behavior: <think> adoption drops from 60% to 18%, while the conditional harm rate remains comparable (39% to 42%).

Connection to Displacement Structure.

The two-channel split connects to the displacement analysis in Appendix D.3. 7B displacement is unidirectional, so constraining M1M_{1} collapses the entire displacement profile and the model reverts to base-model behavior with restored safety at both output and reasoning levels. 3B displacement is sign-mixed and distributed, so the penalty constrains the output decision but not the reasoning trace. Restoring internal reasoning safety may require constraints beyond a single-direction penalty.

E.3 Failure Mode Taxonomy

Table 20 categorizes all 300 responses for each configuration into the following taxonomy. Refuse responses are subdivided into five categories. short denotes a brief refusal without reasoning. think-then-refuse denotes reasoning before refusal. cyclic denotes a repetitive reasoning loop that eventually refuses or is truncated. cyclic+harmful denotes cyclic responses with partial harmful content before truncation. other denotes refusals that do not fit the preceding categories. Fulfill responses are subdivided into three categories. think-then-answer denotes reasoning followed by a harmful answer. crosses-line denotes partial refusal with enough harmful content to be judged as fulfillment. direct denotes immediate harmful compliance.

E.4 Qualitative Examples

We present three examples from different HEx-PHI categories, each showing the same harmful prompt answered by the 7B base model, AM-SFT, and SDP({L15,…,L19}\{\text{L15},\ldots,\text{L19}\}). SDP (7B) restores safety primarily by suppressing extended thinking (§5.2): <think> adoption drops from 60% to 18%. The examples below reflect this pattern: AM-SFT enters reasoning mode and complies; SDP refuses directly without <think>.

Appendix F Reproducibility and Licensing

This section documents the computational resources, software versions, and licensing information for reproducibility.

F.1 Compute and Software

Hardware.

All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Edition GPU (96 GB).

Computational budget.

Table 21 summarizes the GPU hours. Evaluation runs use vLLM inference and take less than 1 GPU-hour per model per benchmark.

Diagnostic cost.

CKA computation, dSd_{S} profiling, and probe training each require a single forward pass over 300 to 600 prompts. Direction extraction requires vLLM generation of incorrect solutions for approximately 2,200 problems. Total diagnostic GPU time is approximately 2 hours. In the realized path, 7B required no expansion, whereas 3B used one compensation diagnostic and one expanded-scope run (approximately 4 GPU-hours), following approximately 2 GPU-hours of direction and hidden-state/displacement diagnostics; each model–benchmark evaluation required less than 1 GPU-hour. These measurements are specific to the reported hardware and do not estimate architecture-independent cost.

Software.

PyTorch 2.9.1, Transformers 4.57.6, PEFT 0.18.1, scikit-learn 1.8.0, Accelerate 1.12.0, vLLM 0.15.1.

Code availability.

Code and data will be released upon publication.

F.2 Artifact Licenses and Ethical Use

Licenses.

Table 22 lists the license for each artifact.

Intended use.

All artifacts are used for their intended purpose: models for fine-tuning research, reasoning datasets for training, and safety benchmarks for evaluation. Our code will implement the SDP training pipeline and diagnostic tools for safety research.

Offensive content and privacy.

HEx-PHI and AdvBench contain harmful prompts by design for safety evaluation; we do not redistribute these datasets. AM-DeepSeek was screened for harmful content via keyword matching, flagging 1.5% of examples, nearly all involving scientific terminology rather than harmful instructions, as reported in Appendix A.2. No personally identifiable information is present in any dataset used.
